opening.headline: The same background is explained again and again, and you learn how to solve problems where the latest information is answered incorrectly by dividing them into project, personalization, and web search.
body: Every time you open a new conversation on ChatGPT, you may have the experience of describing your brand tone and audience from the beginning. Also, when asked about the latest news, there are cases where the person confidently answers unconfirmed information. Although the two problems appear similar on the surface, their causes are different. One is due to lack of ongoing context, the other is due to not having up-to-date information.

In this lesson, you will compare the role and scope of projects, user instructions, and memory in the context of persistence, and see how web searches in the context of up-to-date information and sources differ from regular conversations. Lastly, we will look at examples of dividing and deploying these functions to content tasks that must maintain the brand tone.
objectives: Can explain the role of project, personalization, and web search functions
Can distinguish between recurring contexts and which features address up-to-date information needs
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

screens.title: Same explanation every time, incorrect and up-to-date information
screens.lead: Let's see what happens in three conversations. When you select each item, the situation and cause unfold.

items.prompt: First conversation: After a long explanation, a usable draft emerges.
items.answer: After a lengthy explanation of your brand's tone, audience, and prohibited expressions, you'll come up with a draft you're happy with. It takes time to explain, but the results are satisfactory.

items.prompt: Second conversation: If you open a new window, I will explain again from the beginning.
items.answer: Next week, if you open a new conversation to do the same thing, the previous explanation will not continue. The same background must be rewritten, and the consistency of the results is shaken due to missing conditions. This is a problem caused by the lack of ongoing context.

items.prompt: Third conversation: Confidently answering the latest news incorrectly
items.answer: I asked about the latest news, and unconfirmed information came back as plausible. This is because a normal conversation creates an answer based on the knowledge the model already has and the context of the conversation. This problem is caused by not retrieving current information.

items.prompt: Are these two problems the same?
items.answer: No. The first two conversations are about ‘where do I store my context’, and the third conversation is about ‘how do I get the latest information from outside?’ If the cause of the problem is different, the functions used will also be different.

screens.outro: First, let's recall the difference between a one-off conversation and a subsequent workspace.

screens.title: Think about it: One-time conversations and subsequent workspaces
screens.lead: Read the questions and think for yourself first. There is no need to submit an answer, and when you select an item, the instructor's thoughts unfold.

items.prompt: Have you ever noticed the difference between a one-time conversation and an ongoing workspace?
items.answer: Once a one-time conversation is over, the context stays within the conversation. A workspace, on the other hand, gathers your files, instructions, and previous chats in one place, giving you the same starting point for your next task. The more repetitive the task is every week, the more noticeable the difference becomes.

items.prompt: Is there something you say over and over again every time you open a new conversation?
items.answer: Common examples include roles, readers, tone, and format. Repeated content can be saved somewhere, but the question is where to save it. Where you save it will depend on whether you need it just for this task, for every conversation, or if it's just a preference you build up over time.

items.prompt: How do I identify questions that require up-to-date information?
items.answer: For questions such as today's news, recent announcements, and whether it is currently in operation, the model's knowledge alone is not enough. Questions like these are a signal that you need current information outside of your stored context.

screens.outro: Now let's compare the three functions that take on the persistence context one by one.

screens.title: Project/User Instructions/Memory
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the role of the feature that assumes the persistence context. In the last tab, you can check the criteria for deciding what content to place where.

visual.alt: Mockup screen showing the structure of project settings and personalization settings

tabs.label: project
tabs.body: A project is a workspace that groups related chats, files, and instructions in one place so that ChatGPT is in sync. Select New project from the sidebar and create a name, icon, and color. Add data by uploading PDFs, spreadsheets, documents, images, or pasting text. The number of files you can upload varies depending on your plan. You can start work on one device and continue it on another, and reuse it for repetitive tasks like weekly research or content drafting.

tabs.label: Project Guidelines
tabs.body: If you open Project settings from the project's more menu, you can write down instructions specific to that project. For example, instructions such as ‘answer concisely and use bullet points’. The documentation explains that project guidelines apply only within that project and take precedence over global user guidelines. Therefore, even if the same person does multiple tasks, each task can have different speaking styles and rules.

tabs.label: User Instructions
tabs.body: User instructions are static instructions where you write down what you want ChatGPT to consider when answering. Save once and it will immediately apply to all chats, including existing ones. On the web and desktop, turn on Enable customization in Personalization in Settings and write down Custom Instructions. The character limit is 1,500 characters for Free and Go, and 5,000 characters for Plus·Pro·Enterprise·Business·Education. You can edit or delete it at any time and it will not be communicated to anyone who views the shared link.

tabs.label: memory
tabs.body: When you turn on Memory, ChatGPT will remember relevant preferences and details from conversations and other sources to reduce repetition. Depending on your plan and region, sources can be past chats, saved memories, user instructions, library files, or content from connected apps like Gmail. You may not remember everything, ChatGPT determines which information is relevant, and your memory may change as the context changes. You can view, edit, or clear the Memory summary in Personalization in Settings.

tabs.label: Where should I put it?
tabs.body: Although the three functions appear to have overlapping roles, they have different scopes. If you need materials and rules specific to this task, place them in the project and project instructions. If there is a tone or title that must always be followed in any conversation, write it down in the user guidelines. Personal preferences that are naturally accumulated during conversation are left to memory. It is safer to specify rules that must be followed in the instructions since only a portion of memory may be available.

screens.outro: Now that we've divided up the persistence context, let's look at web searches that keep you up to date.

screens.title: Web browsing: How is it different from regular conversation?
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the differences between regular conversations and web search conversations.

states.label: normal conversation
states.body: In a normal conversation, the model creates an answer based on the knowledge it already has and the context of the conversation so far. It's sufficient for refining text or explaining concepts, but if you ask the model about information it doesn't know, such as recent news, it may come up with plausible but unfounded answers. Since there is no source link attached to the answer, there are fewer clues to check. Questions like this require a function to retrieve current information rather than a function to store persistent context. On the other hand, web search is not omnipotent, so the guidance, not the web search, is responsible for maintaining the speaking style you have decided on. In actual work, the two branches are often mixed. The point to remember is that when you feel that the answer to a general conversation is wrong, first consider 'Does this question require up-to-date information?'

states.label: web search
states.body: When you search the web, ChatGPT finds current information and responds with links to relevant sources. If your question looks like it requires up-to-date information, it can be searched automatically, or to get started yourself, select View all tools in the conversation and select Search, or type / in the message field and select Search. Selecting a citation opens the source and allows you to view all cited sources at once in Sources. However, the results and citations may be incomplete or out of date, so you should open the source and check if the evidence is correct. Web search is a different feature than sidebar search, which finds chats, projects, and files within your account. If you don't see Search, check the Tools menu in New Conversation, App Updates, Accounts & Workspaces, Usage Limits, and Admin Settings.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the two prongs of the solution, let's put them together into one task.

screens.title: Explanatory example: Content work that maintains the brand tone
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates the process of dividing and arranging functions into the task of writing a weekly newsletter. Select the next arrow to follow the steps.

steps.title: Take a look at the situation
steps.body: A team writes a newsletter for the same brand every week. There is a tone guide document and several past articles. Now, every time I open a new conversation, I take the time to explain the tone and paste past posts. Plus, this week's industry news needs to be accurate. It's a task that brings together two problems: iterative context and up-to-date information.

steps.title: Step 1: Create a project dedicated to your newsletter
steps.body: First, create a newsletter-specific project and add the tone guide and past article files. This way, all chats within this project will be answered based on the same data. Work started on a project can be continued on other devices, so the starting point is the same even if the person in charge changes.

steps.title: Step 2: Divide into ranges and place them
steps.body: Now divide the content into scopes. Tone guides and formats that are ‘required only for newsletter work’ are left in the project guidelines. Project guidelines are safe because they apply only within the project and take precedence over global guidelines. Write down the title or tone of voice you want to keep ‘in any conversation’ in the user guidelines. Repetition preferences that accumulate as you write are left to memory.

steps.title: Step 3: Search the web for the latest news
steps.body: This week's industry news isn't resolved in its saved context. Turn on web searches and ask questions to retrieve current information with links to sources. Then open the cited source and check if the date and content match your answer. It's important not to skip this verification step since it's about putting facts into your newsletter.

steps.title: Step 4: State the rules you must follow
steps.body: Since the memory uses only the parts that are determined to be relevant, if you leave it to the rules that must be followed, you may be left out. Rules that must be followed, such as prohibited expressions or required phrases, are written in user instructions or project guidelines. The guidelines have a character limit, so keep them concise and only to the point. For example, it would be enough to summarize it as 'The reader is a practitioner in their 30s, the sentences should be short, and no exaggeration should be used.' Roles are divided by placing detailed examples in the project file and leaving only the judgment criteria in the instructions.

steps.title: Step 5: Check in Settings
steps.body: Finally, check the user instructions and memory in settings. You can correct or erase misremembered information from the memory summary. Turning off memory and deleting past chats are two different things, and turning it off does not erase past chats. As a rule, personal information or sensitive content should not be included in instructions, memory, or project files.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: In this case, the project was a bundle of materials and rules, user instructions were a fixed guide to all conversations, memory was a preferred way to build up, and web searches were responsible for keeping up-to-date information out there. Although it may seem like the same problem, the key point is that the functions assigned are different depending on the scope and nature. When taking on a new task, placement becomes easier if you ask yourself in that order, ‘Is it needed only for this task, is it needed all the time, or is external information needed?’

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the role of each function in the examples, we will summarize the lesson.

screens.title: Summary: Continuing context and up-to-date information
screens.lead: Let's summarize what we've seen so far. Please read while remembering the ongoing context needed for your work.

paragraphs: Repetitive explanations are reduced in projects, user instructions, and memory. All three functions assume a persistence context, but their scope is different. If you need it only for this task, the project will take care of it, if you need it all the time for every conversation, the memory will take care of the user instructions, and the preferences you build up while talking.

Questions requiring up-to-date information will be answered through a web search, with links to relevant sources. Note that web search is a function for finding current information on the Internet, while sidebar search is a function for finding chats, projects, and files within your account.

User instructions and memory can be viewed, modified or cleared in Settings. Turning off memory does not delete past chats, and it is safer to specify the rules that must be followed in the instructions.

For example, when working on content that maintains the brand tone, the tone guide and past articles can be divided into projects, the titles to be applied in all conversations are divided into user guidelines, accumulated preferences are left to memory, and this week's news can be divided into web searches. Additionally, the rule is not to include sensitive information in instructions and memories.
In this way, if you first determine whether the cause of the problem is ‘lack of context to save’ or ‘lack of external information,’ you will naturally decide which function to use.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Web search results and citations may also be incomplete or out of date. When accuracy is important, open the cited source and check the publication date and content directly.

glossary.def: A workspace that brings together related chats, files, and instructions in one place to keep you on the same page.
These are static prompts that apply immediately to all conversations, writing down what you want ChatGPT to consider when answering.
This feature reduces repetition by remembering your preferences and details. You can review, edit, or delete your summary in Settings.
It is a tool that finds current information on the Internet and answers with a link to the source.
This is a function to find chats, projects, and files in my account. This is a different function from web search.

misconceptions.myth: If you turn on memory, all conversations will be remembered.
misconceptions.fact: Memory does not hold all the details. ChatGPT determines what information is relevant, and memories can change as the context changes.

misconceptions.myth: If you turn off memory, past chats will be deleted.
misconceptions.fact: Turning off memory and deleting past chats are two different things. Even if you turn it off, past chats remain, and if you turn it back on later, new memories can be created from the remaining chats.

misconceptions.myth: Web search and sidebar search are the same function.
misconceptions.fact: Web search finds current information on the Internet, and sidebar search finds chats, projects, and files within your account.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Repeated explanations reduce project, user instructions, and memory.
The need for up-to-date information can be answered through a web search, complete with a link to the source.
Persistence contexts are divided into scopes. This is all you need for a project, all the large screen user instructions, and stacking preferences are memory.
You can check, fix or clear instructions and memory in Settings.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Should I place the background that I explain over and over again: the project, the instructions, or the memory?

checks.q: I want certain speech preferences to apply immediately to all conversations whenever I open a new conversation. Which one is best?
options: Write it down as a fixed guide in Custom Instructions.
Turn on web search to retrieve the tone from the Internet.
Find and paste past chats using sidebar search
Write a description of the tone of the project name.
checks.explain: User guidelines are fixed instructions that apply immediately to all conversations. You can turn it on or off in Personalization in settings.

wrong.1: Web search is a function for up-to-date information and sources, not a function to fix speech.
wrong.2: The sidebar search is for finding chats in my account, so it does not apply language.
wrong.3: A project is a workspace that groups files, chats, and instructions, and is not applied just by writing its name.

checks.intro: Where should I write down my preferences that will apply immediately to all conversations? Choose the right location.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. User instructions are static instructions that apply immediately to all conversations.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Search or project names do not convey speech preferences to all conversations. Think of a device that automatically applies to each new conversation.

checks.q: Put your newsletter tasks in the right order
items: Create a project dedicated to the newsletter and include a tone guide and past articles.
Leave wording preferences to user guidance, repetition preferences to memory.
This week's industry news is retrieved with sources from a web search.
Check memory and instructions in settings and do not include sensitive information.
checks.explain: First, the persistent context is bundled into a project, fixed preferences are left to instructions and memory, up-to-date information is supplemented by search, and finally the settings are checked.
checks.intro: Arrange the overall flow of your newsletter tasks in order.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct. You've caught the pulse of persistent context, fixed preferences, up-to-date information, and last settings checks.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is out of order. The flow is to first decide on context and preferences that will be used for a long time, supplement this week's news through search, and finally check the settings.
